title: A daughter is better
hookLine: the king is disappointed at a daughter; the Buddha says she may do better than a son (SN 3.16)

lines: A WHISPER IN THE KING'S EAR.
cards: King Pasenadi is sitting with the Buddha when a man comes in and whispers in his ear. Queen Mallika has given birth. A daughter.
And the text says it plainly: the king was displeased. It doesn't say why. Some readers point to a world where a son carried the throne and the family line.
The Buddha sees the king's face, and answers it with one short verse, spoken to the king himself, right where he sits.

teach.b: SN 3.16 is just the scene and one verse.
A woman, lord of the people, may turn out better than a man.

teach.h: WISE AND VIRTUOUS, IN HER OWN RIGHT
teach.b: She may be wise and virtuous. And her son may become a hero, a ruler of lands. That's the whole teaching, and it's worth being honest about both halves.
The first half is bold for its setting. In a court where a girl's birth was met with a frown, the Buddha tells the king himself that a daughter may be better than a son. Better, not just as good.
And he says why: wisdom and virtue, qualities of the person, not of the body.

teach.h: SPOKEN IN THE TERMS OF ITS TIME
teach.b: The second half speaks in the terms of its time. The verse praises her as a devoted wife who honors her husband's mother, and as the mother of a son who may rule.

Those were roles the king would recognize, and the verse meets him there. Some modern readers notice that tension, and some Buddhist teachers discuss it openly. Still, the verse was spoken to change a father's face.
The sutta doesn't tell us what the king said next.

And Queen Mallika herself appears elsewhere in the texts as a thoughtful follower of the Buddha; tradition says she started life as the daughter of a garland-maker. A garland-maker's daughter who became a queen.
The birth that disappointed a king is, in a way, her story too.

how: Some Buddhist teachers cite the verse to Pasenadi when discussing the place of women and girls, and some communities read it alongside the nuns' own verses in the Therigatha.

the princess born to King Pasenadi

s: the text says King Pasenadi was displeased at the news
SN 3.16 says it plainly, before the Buddha's verse.
the Buddha says a daughter is as good as a son, no better
the verse says a woman may turn out better than a man.
tradition says Queen Mallika began life as a garland-maker's daughter
a garland-maker's daughter who became a queen, and the mother in this story.

games.q: you're the Buddha, sitting with a king who has just frowned at news of a daughter's birth. what do you say?
o: a woman may turn out better than a man, wise and virtuous.
try for a son next time.
games.why: SN 3.16 has the Buddha speak up right then, to the king himself, naming wisdom and virtue.

practice: Remember something that arrived in your life and wasn't what you wanted, a job, a move, a person you didn't expect to matter, and notice your first reaction, the frown, the way the king frowned.
Now look at what that thing became; maybe it turned out better, maybe it's still unfolding. Either way, breathe, and let a little room open around it.

wordCard.voice: Mallika. Pasenadi's queen, the mother in SN 3.16 whose daughter's birth made the king frown, until the Buddha said a woman may turn out better than a man. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Mallika: jasmine, and the name of Pasenadi's queen, the mother in SN 3.16.
